notes.meaning: Moses and the elders together call on all Israel to obey every command given to them. The elders join Moses because he would soon die, leaving them to guide the nation across the Jordan. Keeping God's commands requires daily care and devotion, as though placing a protective hedge around what He has said.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that the Hebrew text uses the singular word for commandment to represent the whole law, while others suggest two separate introductory speeches were joined together here.

notes.meaning: As soon as the Israelites entered Canaan, they were to set up large stones and coat them with smooth white plaster. On this clear surface they were to write the words of God's law so everyone could read them. This public monument showed that enjoying the fruitful Promised Land depended on keeping their covenant with God.

The people were told to place these plastered stones specifically on Mount Ebal. Ebal was a dry, rocky hill where the curses against disobedience would soon be announced. Placing the law there reminded Israel that breaking God's commands brings serious judgment.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The Samaritan Pentateuch reads Mount Gerizim instead of Mount Ebal, but most scholars conclude that Ebal is the original reading and Gerizim was a Samaritan alteration.

notes.meaning: Israel had to build an altar on the mountain using natural field stones that had never been shaped with iron tools. God wanted pure worship rather than human craft or stonecarving that resembled pagan altars. On this altar they offered burnt offerings, which signified dedicating their entire lives to the Lord.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Archaeologists have found a rough stone altar on Mount Ebal dating near the time of Joshua, contrasting with Canaanite altars that were made of carved stones.

notes.meaning: The people were also to sacrifice peace offerings, eating the meal together and rejoicing before God. These peace offerings celebrated that God had brought them safely across the Jordan and welcomed them into fellowship with Himself. Joy and worship belong together when God's people live in peace with Him.

The words of God's law were to be inscribed clearly and boldly on the plastered stones. God made His standards simple and plain for all people to understand, rather than hiding them away with leaders or priests. A clear display of God's word leaves everyone without an excuse for ignoring it.

Moses and the Levitical priests call the entire assembly to be quiet and listen closely. By renewing this sacred agreement, Israel was stepping forward once again as the chosen people of the Lord. Since they belonged to God, they were obligated to listen to His voice and obey all His commands.

On that very day, Moses gave the instructions for a national ceremony between two mountains. This ceremony would bring every tribe into the presence of God to hear the results of obedience and disobedience. It impressed upon the people that following God was a matter of life and death.

Six tribes were placed on Mount Gerizim to pronounce blessings, and the other six were placed on Mount Ebal to pronounce curses. Green, fertile Gerizim pictured the fruitfulness of obedience, while barren Ebal pictured the penalty of sin. Dividing the tribes this way showed that the whole nation shared responsibility for upholding God's covenant.

The Levites stood in the valley between the mountains and proclaimed the words of the covenant in a loud voice. To each statement, all the people were required to answer with 'Amen,' which means 'so be it.' By saying this word aloud, every Israelite agreed that God's judgments were completely just.

The first curse falls on anyone who crafts an idol and hides it away to worship in secret. Human courts might never catch secret idolatry, but the Lord sees what is hidden and detests all false gods. True worship requires genuine loyalty to God from the inside out.

This curse condemns anyone who treats a father or mother with disrespect or contempt. In God's law, honoring parents comes directly after honoring God Himself. Even private bitterness or hidden mockery against parents brings the Lord's displeasure.

A curse is declared on anyone who quietly shifts a boundary stone to steal a neighbor's property. In Israel, land was a gift from God to each family, making boundary tampering a form of deceitful theft. God hates dishonest gain and expects His people to respect what belongs to others.

This curse warns against misleading a blind person or leading them off the path. It forbids cruel acts against disabled people and also condemns taking advantage of anyone who is helpless or in the dark. God's people are called to guide and protect the vulnerable rather than cause them to stumble.

God places under a curse anyone who denies justice to foreigners, orphans, or widows. Because these people had no social influence or wealth to defend themselves, dishonest judges and neighbors might easily take advantage of them. God acts as the personal protector of the weak and promises to punish those who wrong them.

This curse falls on any man who has sexual relations with his father's wife, which violates his father's marriage honor. Such incest breaks God's design for family purity and destroys trust in the home. God demands moral purity in family relationships even when no one else is watching.

A curse is spoken against anyone who engages in sexual acts with an animal. This unnatural sin degrades the human dignity God gave to people and violates the created order. The entire congregation answered 'Amen' to show their rejection of such corrupt behavior.

This curse condemns anyone who commits incest by having sexual relations with his sister or half-sister. God established families to be places of safety and honor rather than sinful desire. The people's agreed response showed that the whole nation stood behind God's rules for family holiness.

A curse is pronounced on anyone who has sexual relations with his mother-in-law. This was another forbidden incestuous act that broke family boundaries and destroyed domestic trust in secret. God's law protects the dignity and peace of extended family relations.

This curse targets anyone who strikes down a neighbor in secret, covering up murder so human authorities cannot find it. Commentators note that it also applies to backbiting and slander that secretly ruins someone's life. Human courts may fail to discover hidden attacks, but God sees every wrong and will judge it.

A curse rests on anyone who takes money to kill an innocent person, whether as a hired killer, a lying witness, or a corrupt judge. Selling an innocent life for profit is a dreadful crime that destroys true justice. God requires His people to treat human life as sacred and beyond any price.

The final curse brings all the commands together by condemning anyone who fails to practice every word of God's law. Because the law requires full and constant obedience, this verse reveals that every human falls short and stands under a curse. Christian writers emphasize that this shows our need for Jesus Christ, who saved believers by taking the curse of the law upon Himself.
